Q: Why does mainAxisAlignment not show any effect (no errors)? A:

Actually by default Row and Column will not occupy full width or Height by default at mainAxisAlignment.

Wrap the inner Row or Column with Expanded widget to occupy full width or height and then proceed to use it.

Q: How to keep a “global” React Error Boundary config but only show fallback locally? A:

You can't achieve this with only a single error boundary. If you only use one error boundary at the root of your app, then that is where errors will be caught and "handled". You can use as many error boundaries as you like/feel is necessary. In other words, you can create an error boundary around specific components if you want to catch and handle errors at that boundary and leave components higher up the React tree alone.

Q: Changing column values based on values of separate columns A:

I prefer short solutions (because for me, they are easier to understand later, when I would need that code). So here is a 3-line version. LL is a named array with column-names as well as row-names. It has a similar role as in the @margusl's answer.

library(dplyr)

LL = cbind(brown = c(3,6,Inf), rainbow=c(3,5,Inf), coho = c(2,6,Inf))
rownames(LL) = c("Yoy","Age1","Age2+")
> LL
      brown rainbow coho
Yoy       3       3    2
Age1      6       5    6
Age2+   Inf     Inf  Inf

To add the new column we subset the corresponding column in LL by name, then take the name of the first row that is greater or equal to the Length_in.

df |> rowwise() |> mutate(Category = names(which(LL[,Species] >= Length_in))[1])

The result:

# A tibble: 60 × 4
# Rowwise: 
   Species Length_in Age   Category
   <chr>       <int> <chr> <chr>   
 1 rainbow         9 yoy   Age2+   
 2 coho            4 adult Age1    
 3 brown           7 yoy   Age2+   
 4 rainbow         1 adult Yoy     
 5 coho            2 yoy   Yoy     
 6 brown          13 adult Age2+   
 7 rainbow        11 yoy   Age2+   
 8 coho            3 adult Age1    
 9 brown           8 yoy   Age2+   
10 rainbow        12 adult Age2+   
# ℹ 50 more rows
# ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

Q: Python type hinting without cyclic imports A:

It will be interesting to note that with the release of Python 3.14, in Oct. 2026, this problem is "gone" -

All annotations are now lazily evaluated by default - one doesn't even need the from __future__ import annotations, from PEP-563 maneuver that was (and is) available since Python 3.7 - which would convert all annotations to strings, and require explicit access at runtime for being evaluated. That approach is now obsoleted.

The example snippets would need to be rewritten so that the main module can be imported from mymixin even if its contents are not in-place, and one can use dotted access to get to the Main attribute in the main module:

mymixin.py


from . import main

...

class MyMixin(object):
    def func2(self: main.Main, xxx):  # <--- note the type hint
        ...

The main.Main attribute can be used in annotations, even though it doesn't exist at the time the def func2(self: main.Main, xxx): is evaluated.

With the new default annotation behavior in Python 3.14, annotations are kept as lazy internal objects, which are transparently evaluated at runtime only if needed - and no different semantics, or typing, or anything is needed for anyone making use of annotations for other purposes than static typing (Like dataclasses and Pydantic do - although, I believe one will still find issues if trying to make use of cyclic imports for dataclasses relying solely on this behavior in Python 3.14 - that is subject to testing)

Upcoming: explicit lazy imports

Note that for Python 3.15 (scheduled release for Oct. 2026), there will be a new lazy import modifier which will allow the xxx to be imported directly. (It will just work due to Deferred evaluation also been in place from Python 3.14, but that is now the default).

Anyway, for Python 3.15 (should already work with alpha builds):

mymixin.py


lazy from .main import Main

...

class MyMixin(object):
    def func2(self: Main, xxx):  # <--- note the type hint
        ...

Q: How do I return a Float32Array from a function? A:

SomeFunction is async, so you'll have to secondsArray = await SomeFunction(); to get the promise's value (or use .then() chains, etc. if you can't make the calling function async).
